title: Search in Rotated Sorted Array II
notes:
Task and constraints: Search for target in a rotated sorted array that may contain duplicates. Return whether the target occurs.
Idea: Use binary search. If the middle value matches, succeed. If left, middle, and right values are equal, trim both ends; otherwise identify the sorted half and keep the half whose range can contain target.
Technique and why it applies: A sorted half still supports range-based elimination, but duplicates can make the sorted side ambiguous and require cautious boundary trimming.
Invariant: If target exists, at least one possible occurrence remains inside the current interval.
Edge cases: Many equal values can force linear behavior; unlike the distinct-value version, logarithmic worst-case time is not guaranteed.
Complexity: Average time is O(log n), worst-case O(n). Extra space is O(1).
time_complexity: O(log n) average, O(n) worst case
complexity_reason: Ambiguous duplicate boundaries may be removed one at a time.

title: Remove Duplicates from Sorted List II
notes:
Task and constraints: Remove every value that occurs more than once in a sorted linked list, leaving only values that appeared exactly once.
Idea: Use a dummy head and a predecessor pointer. If the next two nodes share a value, advance past the entire run; otherwise advance the predecessor by one node.
Technique and why it applies: Sorting makes every occurrence of a duplicated value contiguous, so one run can be skipped completely.
Invariant: The list before prev contains only values known to occur once; prev is the tail of that retained prefix.
Edge cases: Duplicates may start at the original head or occupy the entire list. A dummy node handles both cases uniformly.
Complexity: Time is O(n) because each node is traversed a constant number of times. Extra space is O(1).
complexity_reason: The predecessor and current-run pointers traverse the list in place.

title: Remove Duplicates from Sorted List
notes:
Task and constraints: In a sorted linked list, retain one node for each distinct value and remove later duplicates.
Idea: Walk through the list. If the current node and its successor have equal values, bypass the successor; otherwise advance to the successor.
Technique and why it applies: Sorted order places duplicates next to one another, so only adjacent comparisons are needed.
Invariant: The processed prefix contains one node per distinct value and remains sorted.
Edge cases: Empty and one-node lists require no changes. Consecutive duplicate runs are removed by repeatedly checking the same current node after a bypass.
Complexity: Time is O(n). Extra space is O(1).
complexity_reason: Each node is visited and bypassed at most a constant number of times.

title: Largest Rectangle in Histogram
notes:
Task and constraints: Find the largest rectangle area under a histogram of unit-width bars with non-negative heights.
Idea: Maintain indices of bars in increasing height order. When a lower bar arrives, pop taller bars and calculate the maximal width for each popped height using the new index and the previous stack top.
Technique and why it applies: The first lower bar to the right and the previous lower bar to the left bound the widest rectangle with a popped bar's height.
Invariant: Stack indices have non-decreasing heights, and each popped bar is finalized at its first lower right boundary.
Edge cases: Append a zero-height sentinel to flush the stack. Empty histograms return zero.
Complexity: Time is O(n) because each index is pushed and popped once. Extra space is O(n).
complexity_reason: Every histogram index enters and leaves the monotonic stack at most once.

title: Maximal Rectangle
approach_name: Build row heights and solve histogram
notes:
Task and constraints: Find the largest all-ones rectangle in a binary matrix.
Idea: Treat each row as the base of a histogram. Maintain heights[c], the consecutive number of ones ending at the current row, resetting a height to zero for a zero cell. For each row, calculate the largest histogram rectangle.
Technique and why it applies: Any all-ones rectangle ending at a row corresponds to a rectangle under that row's histogram heights.
Invariant: After updating a row, heights[c] equals the vertical run of ones ending at that cell.
Edge cases: Empty matrices return zero. Rows containing zeroes split possible rectangles at those columns.
Complexity: Time is O(mn), as each row's histogram is processed linearly. Extra space is O(n).
complexity_reason: Each row updates n histogram heights and performs one O(n) stack scan.

title: Partition List
approach_name: Build stable less-than and greater groups
notes:
Task and constraints: Reorder a linked list so values smaller than x appear before values at least x, preserving relative order within each group.
Idea: Build two lists with dummy heads, appending each existing node to the less-than list or the greater/equal list. Connect the first list to the second at the end.
Technique and why it applies: Separate stable passes preserve the original relative order of nodes within both partitions.
Invariant: Each partial list contains the encountered nodes of its category in original order, and each input node is placed in exactly one list.
Edge cases: Either partition may be empty. Terminate the greater/equal tail to avoid retaining an old link that forms a cycle.
Complexity: Time is O(n). Extra space is O(1) beyond a fixed number of dummy nodes.
complexity_reason: Nodes are relinked into two stable lists using fixed pointers.
code:
from typing import Optional

class Solution:
    def partition(self, head: Optional[ListNode], x: int) -> Optional[ListNode]:
        less=ListNode(0);greater=ListNode(0);a,b=less,greater
        while head:
            nxt=head.next;head.next=None
            if head.val<x:a.next=head;a=head
            else:b.next=head;b=head
            head=nxt
        a.next=greater.next
        return less.next

title: Scramble String
notes:
Task and constraints: Decide whether one string can be transformed into another by recursively splitting a string into two non-empty parts and optionally swapping the two parts at any split.
Idea: For each pair of substrings, first compare equality and character frequencies. Try every split in both aligned and swapped arrangements; memoize each substring pair.
Technique and why it applies: Every scramble must arise from some split point, and the two recursive subproblems cover the corresponding parts in either order.
Invariant: A memoized state is true exactly when its two substrings have a valid scramble relation.
Edge cases: Unequal lengths fail immediately. Character-frequency mismatch prunes impossible states before exploring splits.
Complexity: The memoized recurrence is O(n^4) time in the straightforward substring implementation and O(n^3) states, with substring storage adding overhead.
space_complexity: O(n^3) memo states, with substring/key overhead
complexity_reason: There are O(n^3) substring pairs and each state tries O(n) splits with linear frequency checks.

title: Merge Sorted Array
notes:
Task and constraints: Merge two sorted arrays into nums1, which already has enough trailing capacity for all values. The first m entries of nums1 and all n entries of nums2 are valid inputs.
Idea: Compare the largest remaining values and write the larger one at the end of nums1, moving backward until nums2 is exhausted.
Technique and why it applies: Writing from the back avoids overwriting unread values in nums1.
Invariant: Positions after the write pointer contain the largest values from both arrays in sorted order.
Edge cases: If nums2 is empty, nums1 is already correct. If nums1's valid prefix is empty, copy all of nums2.
Complexity: Time is O(m+n). Extra space is O(1).
complexity_reason: Each input element is read once and output is written into nums1.

title: Gray Code
notes:
Task and constraints: Return a sequence of all n-bit Gray codes starting at zero, where adjacent values differ in exactly one bit.
Idea: For each bit width, reflect the existing sequence in reverse order and set the new high bit on each reflected value. Equivalently, value i maps to i XOR (i shifted right by one).
Technique and why it applies: The XOR formula transforms ordinary binary counting into Gray code, changing only one bit between consecutive indices.
Invariant: The sequence contains each n-bit code once and consecutive values differ in one bit.
Edge cases: n=0 conventionally yields [0], though the constraints may start at one. The sequence begins with zero.
Complexity: Time is O(2^n). Extra space is O(2^n) for the returned list.
complexity_reason: Every code is generated once and stored in the output.

title: Subsets II
approach_name: Sort and skip equal sibling choices
notes:
Task and constraints: Return all unique subsets of an array that may contain duplicate values. The empty subset is included.
Idea: Sort the array and backtrack by choosing the next element from a start index. Skip a value when it equals the previous value at the same recursion depth.
Technique and why it applies: Sorting groups duplicates, and sibling-level skipping prevents equivalent subsets while still allowing repeated values to appear in a subset.
Invariant: The path is a subset of the processed prefix, indices increase, and duplicate sibling branches are not explored.
Edge cases: An empty input returns a list containing the empty subset. Multiple equal values may still appear together if they occupy different positions.
Complexity: Time is O(n·2^n) worst case for copying subsets. Auxiliary space is O(n), excluding output.
complexity_reason: There are at most 2^n subsets and each output copy can contain n values.
